{{family name hatnote|[[Shī (surname)|Shi]]|lang=Chinese}}
'''Wanxiong Shi''' ({{zh|c=施皖雄|p=Shī Wǎnxióng|poj=Si Oán-hiông}}; 6 October 1963 - 30 September 2021) was a Chinese mathematician. He was known for his fundamental work in the theory of [[Ricci flow]].

== Education ==
Shi was a native of [[Quanzhou]], [[Fujian]]. In 1978, Shi graduated from Quanzhou No. 5 Middle School, and entered the [[University of Science and Technology of China]]. Shi earned his bachelor's degree in mathematics in 1982, then he went to the Institute of Mathematics of [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] and obtained his master's degree in mathematics in 1985 under the guidance of [[Lu Qikeng]] ({{zh|陆启铿}}) and [[Zhong Jiaqing]] ({{zh|钟家庆}}). Then Shi was recruited by [[Shing-Tung Yau]] to study under him at the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Shape of a Life: One Mathematician's Search for the Universe's Hidden Geometry|author1=Shing-Tung Yau|author2=Steve Nadis|publisher=Yale University Press|year=2019|isbn=9780300245523|page=171}}</ref> In 1987, Shi followed Yau to [[Harvard University]] and obtained his Ph.D. there in 1990.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://math.ustc.edu.cn/2021/1009/c18650a525056/page.htm|title=才学一流 破百年猜想 贡献卓著 人生几何 解千古疑惑 淡泊超然|website=School of Mathematical Sciences USTC|date=9 October 2021|accessdate=7 May 2022}}</ref>

Since Shi was stronger in [[geometric analysis]] than other Chinese students, having an impressive ability to carry out highly technical arguments, he was assigned by Yau to investigate Ricci flow in the challenging case of noncompact [[Riemannian manifold|manifolds]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/lzKEN4CSN99vih1QViMquA|title=忆皖雄同学|author=郑方阳 Zheng Fangyang|website= Wechat official accounts platform|date=6 October 2021|accessdate=7 May 2022}}</ref> Shi made significant breakthroughs and was highly regarded by researchers in the field. [[Richard S. Hamilton|Richard Hamilton]], the founder of Ricci flow theory, liked his work very much.<ref name=yau/>

== Academic career and later life ==
Upon his graduation, several prominent universities were interested in offering him a faculty position. [[Hung-Hsi Wu]] ({{zh|伍鸿熙}}) from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] asked Yau if Shi could come to Berkeley. Without seeking opinion from Yau, Shi applied to and got tenure track assistant professorship offers from the [[University of California, San Diego]], where Richard Hamilton was working at, and [[Purdue University]].

Shi decided to join Purdue University. He published several important papers there, and was awarded three grants from the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] in 1991, 1994 and 1997.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=9103140&HistoricalAwards=false|title=Award Abstract # 9103140 Mathematical Sciences: "Studying the Topology of Riemannian Manifolds through Ricci Deformation of the Metric"|publisher=National Science Foundation|date=10 May 1991|accessdate=9 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=9403405&HistoricalAwards=false|title=Award Abstract # 9403405 Mathematical Sciences: Heat Flow on Riemannian Manifolds|publisher=National Science Foundation|date=13 July 1994|accessdate=9 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=9703656&HistoricalAwards=false|title=Award Abstract # 9703656 Global Analysis on Riemannian Manifolds|publisher=National Science Foundation|date=14 February 1997|accessdate=9 May 2022}}</ref> However, Shi did not pass the tenure review in 1997, so he had to leave the university. (The principal investigator of the NSF grant of 1997 was changed because of this.) Yau believes that the failure was due to the faculty members not realising the importance of Ricci flow theory. Hamilton sent a belated reference letter to Purdue University in which he rebuked the decision, but to no avail.<ref name=yau>{{cite web|title=丘成桐：悼念我的学生施皖雄 |author=Shing-Tung Yau|url=https://www.sohu.com/a/493750157_686587|website=sohu.com|date=7 October 2021|accessdate=7 May 2022}}</ref>

Shi then left academia and moved to Washington D.C., where he lived a frugal and secluded life in solitude, and had less and less contact with his friends. He turned down some offers from other universities.<ref name=yau/> Yau and former classmates of Shi tried to persuade Shi and help him return to academia, but he rejected.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/qKEEYte3VV5rwYr1132NRg|title=【情系科大】特立独行，不离不弃——怀念皖雄同学|author = 王晓林 Wang Xiaolin|website= Wechat official accounts platform|date=12 October 2021|accessdate=7 May 2022}}</ref> Yau felt sorry for Shi's leaving academia, since among the four students of Yau who worked on Ricci flow, Shi had done the best work. Shi died from a sudden heart attack in the evening of September 30, 2021.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_14803081|title=58岁数学家施皖雄去世，曾为解决庞加莱猜想做出基础性贡献|website=thepaper.cn|date=7 October 2021|accessdate=7 May 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.shkjb.com/cont/811/218469.html|title=师友追忆旅美数学家施皖雄——"我们一起生活，对于将来是荣幸的"|publisher=上海科技报 Shanghai Keji Bao|date=21 October 2021|accessdate=7 May 2022}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

== Work ==
Shi initiated the study of Ricci flow theory on noncompact complete manifolds. He proved local derivative estimates for the Ricci flow, which are fundamental to many arguments of the theory, including [[Gregory Perelman|Perelman]]'s proof of the [[Poincaré conjecture]] using Ricci flow in 2002.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ims.cuhk.edu.hk/activities/yau/speech/hamilton_en.html|title=Prof. Hamilton's speech about Poincare conjecture in Beijing (8 June, 2005)|author=Richard S. Hamilton|website=The Institute of Mathematical Sciences, CUHK|accessdate=7 May 2022}}</ref>
